title: The Dahlia Above Plot Twelve
subtitle: The greenhouse stayed locked. Someone simply reached farther.
brief: On judging morning, the single prize bloom of Hearthside's midnight dahlia was found neatly removed from its stem. The rooftop greenhouse door was still tied with the chairperson's numbered paper seal.
Only three early visitors were on the community-centre roof. None had the greenhouse key, and each insists they stayed outside the railing around Plot Twelve.
question: Who removed the dahlia, and how did they reach it without opening the greenhouse?

suspects.name: Mara Sen
suspects.statement: I checked the door seal from the stairwell, then went downstairs to fetch the ribbons.

suspects.name: Theo Brook
suspects.statement: I recorded swifts from the far parapet. My equipment never went near Plot Twelve.

suspects.name: Elsie Quill
suspects.statement: I delivered empty vases at six and left them beside the lift. I had no cutting tools.

theories.label: Reached through the roof louver with a telescoping litter picker and pulled the bloom out
Opened the sealed door with a duplicate key, then replaced the paper seal
Cut the flower the previous evening and propped it on the stem until morning

clues.title: One unbroken number
clues.text: Seal 041 is genuine, its gum is fully dry, and its fibres remain continuous across the door gap. The greenhouse door did not open after closing.

clues.title: A gap above the bloom
clues.text: A twenty-two-centimetre-wide ventilation louver stands directly above the dahlia. Its insect screen is unhooked at one corner. The fourteen-centimetre bloom is 1.8 metres below it; the picker's closed head is nine centimetres, so both fit through the opening.

clues.title: Crushed, not clipped
clues.text: The stem ends in two opposing crescent dents. Sharp shears would leave a flat slice; padded gripping jaws made this crushed break.

clues.title: Yellow in the green
clues.text: A fleck of yellow closed-cell foam clings to the broken stem. Theo's telescoping litter picker has yellow foam lining both jaws.

clues.title: The recording moved
clues.text: Theo's 6:12 swift recording contains the greenhouse vent fan at full volume, not the distant parapet wind. A red dahlia petal is folded inside his picker's telescoping joint.

hints: Treat the intact door seal as reliable. Look for an opening meant for air rather than people.
The shape of the damage identifies a gripping tool, and one suspect brought an extendable one to the roof.

solution.title: The flower was taken at arm's length.
solution.explanation: Theo unhooked one corner of the louver's insect screen, lowered his telescoping litter picker, gripped the fourteen-centimetre dahlia through the padded jaws, and drew it back through the twenty-two-centimetre opening. The door seal is truly intact. The twin crescent dents and yellow foam identify the tool, while the loud vent fan and trapped petal place Theo and his picker beside the greenhouse rather than at the far parapet.
proof: The roof louver bypasses the sealed door
Padded jaws explain the paired crush marks
Theo's recording and picker carry traces from the scene

title: The Moustache in Cobalt
subtitle: A portrait was defaced without touching a drop of paint.
brief: Minutes before the neighbourhood portrait show opened, a sweeping blue moustache appeared across Mrs. D'Souza's painted face. The frame's signed hanging wire and all four backing seals were intact.
The artist insists the portrait was clean at three o'clock. Three exhibitors crossed the little gallery before the mark was noticed.
question: Who added the moustache, and how was the sealed portrait left unharmed?

suspects.name: Mara D'Souza
suspects.statement: It is my grandmother's portrait. I checked the paint, glass, and seals before hanging it.

suspects.name: Felix Ward
suspects.statement: I dusted the frames with a dry cloth. I never unsealed Mara's backing board.

suspects.name: Kit Rowan
suspects.statement: I pinned up children's drawings. I did not touch the serious portraits.

theories.label: Drew on the outside of the glazing with washable window crayon
Slipped a painted transparent sheet between the frame and portrait
Painted the moustache on the portrait before the backing seals were signed

clues.title: Four honest seals
clues.text: Every backing seal bears matching paper fibres and Mara's continuous signature. No sheet or brush entered from behind after the frame was closed.

clues.title: A face that slips sideways
clues.text: Viewed from the far left, the blue curve shifts a few millimetres away from the painted upper lip. The mark sits on a surface in front of the portrait.

clues.title: A blue crumb
clues.text: A soft cobalt crumb rests against the outer frame lip. It smears under a damp cotton bud while the varnished painting beneath remains untouched.

clues.title: Made for windows
clues.text: The mark contains wax, soap, and washable dye rather than artist's oil pigment. It matches the window crayons used in the children's cartoon workshop.

clues.title: Cobalt at the glass
clues.text: Kit signed out the only cobalt window crayon at 3:08. A 3:24 setup time-lapse shows it in Kit's hand against Mrs. D'Souza's glass while Felix dusts the opposite wall and Mara staffs the lobby. Kit returned it at 3:37 with its tip flattened into the moustache's broad curve.

hints: Move your viewpoint. If two marks shift relative to one another, they are not on the same plane.
The backing seals protect the painting, but they do not protect the outside face of the glass.

solution.title: The joke was only glass-deep.
solution.explanation: Kit drew the moustache directly on the outside of the glazing with the cartoon workshop's cobalt window crayon. Parallax separates the mark from the painted face, and the washable wax-and-soap pigment confirms that the portrait itself was never defaced. The time-lapse places the signed-out crayon in Kit's hand at the glass while the other suspects are elsewhere, and its newly flattened tip matches the curve.
proof: Parallax places the mark in front of the painting
The pigment is washable window crayon
The time-lapse shows Kit holding the matching crayon at the glass

title: The Lantern That Would Not Light
subtitle: The oil was sound. The wick had been dressed for another job.
brief: The festival's lead lantern passed its afternoon test, yet refused to light when the river procession began at 7:20. Its reservoir was full, the air holes were open, and a fresh-looking wick sat in the burner.
Three volunteers worked around the lantern table after the successful test. One replaced a useful piece of cotton with something that only looked like it.
question: Who disabled the lead lantern, and what was substituted for its wick?

suspects.name: Lian Park
suspects.statement: I tested the real wick at four. After that, I only repaired the paper shade.

suspects.name: Niko Bell
suspects.statement: I tightened my drum in the music tent. I never handled the lantern burners.

suspects.name: Bea Moss
suspects.statement: I left beeswax candles on the table, but wax near a wick is hardly suspicious.

theories.label: Replaced the cotton wick with shellacked drum cord that could not draw oil
Diluted the reservoir with water so fuel could not reach the flame
Sealed the air vents with clear wax so the flame suffocated

clues.title: Good oil, open air
clues.text: A spoonful from the reservoir burns cleanly, and a wire passes through every vent. Neither watered fuel nor blocked airflow caused the failure.

clues.title: Cotton that will not bend
clues.text: The supposed wick is glossy and rigid. After ten minutes in oil, its core remains dry instead of darkening by capillary action.

clues.title: Amber at the cut
clues.text: A cut cross-section reveals cotton cord sealed beneath amber shellac. Beeswax would soften with hand warmth; this coating does not.

clues.title: The red tracer
clues.text: Niko's drum-repair cord uses the same three-strand braid, amber shellac, and single red tracer thread as the false wick. Twelve centimetres are missing from his spool.

clues.title: A reflection in brass
clues.text: A 7:14 group photo—six minutes before the first lighting attempt—reflects Niko beside the burner tray, holding the lantern's brass wick cap. Lian and Bea are visible together across the square.

hints: A wick must carry fuel as well as resemble cotton. Check whether this one absorbs anything.
The hard amber coating belongs to an instrument-repair material, not to the beekeeper's soft wax.

solution.title: The false wick was tuned, not woven.
solution.explanation: Niko removed the tested wick and replaced it with a short length of shellacked drum cord before the 7:20 lighting attempt. The cord looked like braided cotton but its hard coating prevented oil from rising to the flame. Its weave, red tracer, and amber shellac match Niko's missing repair cord exactly, and the 7:14 photograph places the wick cap in his hand during the available interval.
proof: The fuel and air supply both work
Shellac prevents the false wick from absorbing oil
The matching cord and photograph identify Niko

title: The Silver Thimble
subtitle: The cabinet never opened. Its dust travelled toward the wall.
brief: Rosebank's engraved centennial thimble vanished from a locked wall cabinet before the quilting circle arrived. The glass door's wax seal was undisturbed, and the nineteen-millimetre thimble was too wide for any eight-millimetre slot in the rear vent's apparently fixed mesh.
Three people entered the stitching room that morning. Each knew the heirloom would be photographed at ten.
question: Who removed the thimble, and how did it pass mesh slots narrower than the object itself?

suspects.name: June Alder
suspects.statement: I dusted and vacuumed the room. The display cabinet and my vacuum hose were never connected.

suspects.name: Ruth Webb
suspects.statement: I arranged fabric beneath the cabinet, then fetched tea before anyone else arrived.

suspects.name: Leo Finch
suspects.statement: I measured the light and unpacked my tripod. I never touched the display.

theories.label: Loosened the vent mesh and used suction to pull the thimble into a vacuum hose
Removed the cabinet hinge pin and lifted the sealed glass door away as one piece
Pushed a sticky rod through the keyhole and drew the thimble to the lock

clues.title: The door stayed shut
clues.text: The wax bridges glass and frame without a crack. Both hinge pins retain old oxidation, and the keyhole's dust is undisturbed.

clues.title: A curved clean trail
clues.text: Dust forms a swept arc from the thimble's plinth to the rear vent. A loose red thread from the display points along the same route.

clues.title: A larger opening behind the slots
clues.text: Each fixed-looking mesh slot is only eight millimetres wide, but the whole mesh is a removable fifty-five-millimetre cassette. Its two lower clips are freshly bent outward, exposing an aperture wide enough for June's thirty-four-millimetre nozzle.

clues.title: Felt in the elbow
clues.text: June's nozzle has a twenty-six-millimetre inner bore, wide enough for the nineteen-millimetre thimble. Red display felt and silver-polish dust coat its interior, and something metallic rattles beyond the hose elbow.

clues.title: Three minutes of suction
clues.text: The hall vacuum's service meter advanced by three minutes after June signed the room clean. The thimble is lodged behind its hose filter, wrapped harmlessly in red thread.

hints: The thimble did not need to fit through the fixed mesh if the mesh itself could be moved.
Follow the direction of the dust and thread. Both point toward a tool that moves objects with air.

solution.title: The heirloom took a very short vacuum journey.
solution.explanation: June bent back the vent cassette's lower clips, lifted the whole mesh away from its fifty-five-millimetre aperture, and inserted the vacuum nozzle. Its twenty-six-millimetre bore admitted the nineteen-millimetre thimble, which suction dragged across the felt and into the hose. She then replaced the mesh, leaving the sealed glass door untouched. The dust trail, bent clips, felt inside her nozzle, and thimble behind the hose filter establish one continuous route.
proof: The cabinet door and keyhole were never disturbed
Dust and thread trace a route to the loosened vent
June's nozzle and hose contain the display traces and thimble

title: The Moon That Tore Itself
subtitle: The workshop was empty when the scenery began to move.
brief: A hand-painted canvas moon was locked inside the theatre workshop at four. When the director opened the room at 4:35, a fresh tear ran from the moon's lower edge almost to its centre. The numbered door tape was intact.
Three cast members handled the scenery before lockup. The damage happened later, in a room with no person inside but one machine still following its schedule.
question: Who rigged the tear, and what movement triggered it after the room was locked?

suspects.name: Priya Lake
suspects.statement: I retouched the moon, photographed the clean canvas, and sealed my paint box before four.

suspects.name: Milo Hart
suspects.statement: I returned my coat to wardrobe. I never touched a pulley or the painted moon.

suspects.name: Ren Ortiz
suspects.statement: I locked the controls after programming the routine safety cycle. No manual cue ran.

theories.label: Hooked a sharp costume brooch to the neighbouring fly line so its scheduled movement tore the canvas
Applied fast-shrinking paint that pulled the canvas apart as it dried
Hid a clockwork blade behind the moon and timed it to open after lockup

clues.title: An empty workshop
clues.text: The numbered tape is original and unbroken. A corridor camera shows nobody entering between 4:00 and 4:35, so the damage was prepared before lockup.

clues.title: Pulled from behind
clues.text: Canvas fibres curl toward the audience side while the tear climbs upward. A sharp point caught the back lower edge and was hauled vertically.

clues.title: Silver in the fibres
clues.text: The tear holds the broken point of a steel brooch pin and fine silver stage glitter. There is no blade housing, spring oil, or unusual paint shrinkage.

clues.title: One crescent on the line
clues.text: Milo's understudy coat is missing its glittered crescent brooch. The broken crescent body and clasp remain tied to the neighbouring fly line; their snapped pin fits the steel point embedded in the canvas.

clues.title: The 4:27 safety rise
clues.text: Priya's timestamped 3:58 photo of the clean canvas reflects Milo behind the moon tying black thread at that line while Ren locks the control cage. At 4:27, the automatic safety cycle raised the same line by eighty centimetres.

hints: An intact door means the culprit arranged a delayed action before four o'clock.
Match the direction of the tear to the only object in the empty room that moved upward on schedule.

solution.title: The moon tore on cue.
solution.explanation: Before lockup, Milo tied his sharp crescent brooch to the neighbouring fly line and hooked its pin into the moon's lower back edge. Priya's 3:58 photo catches him tying the line while Ren locks the controls. The programmed 4:27 safety cycle then raised the line, snapping the brooch pin and dragging its point upward through the canvas while the workshop remained empty. The recovered brooch body, embedded point, photograph, and fly log reconstruct the delayed sabotage.
proof: The sealed room requires a prepared delayed action
The upward tear follows the scheduled fly-line movement
The 3:58 photograph places Milo rigging the recovered brooch

title: The Vanishing Letter Q
subtitle: The tile bag held a perfect count and one piece that was never wood.
brief: Officials counted one hundred wooden tiles into a canvas bag, weighed it, and sealed the drawstring before the neighbourhood word-game final. When play began, the letter Q was missing. The seal remained intact.
A cup of tea had spilled across the bag while the finalists took their seats. Everyone assumed the damp patch was merely bad luck.
question: Who made the Q disappear from a sealed bag, and what temporary substitute fooled the count?

suspects.name: Celia Crumb
suspects.statement: I brought refreshments and read out the tile count. I never added anything to the bag.

suspects.name: Owen Reed
suspects.statement: I pulled the seal tight myself. The correct weight was written down before the spill.

suspects.name: Nora Vale
suspects.statement: I fetched score sheets from the next room. The tiles were already on the counting cloth.

theories.label: Removed the wooden Q before sealing and replaced it with a hollow painted sugar tile matched to its weight
Worked the Q into a concealed pocket inside the bag's double seam
Pulled a metal-backed Q through the canvas with a magnet beneath the table

clues.title: A correct count and weight
clues.text: At 2:44 the bag held one hundred tile-shaped pieces at the expected total weight on the officials' whole-gram scale. The original string seal has not moved since that measurement.

clues.title: Sticky inside, clean outside
clues.text: The tea dried normally on the outer canvas, but the lining beneath it is tacky and slightly sweet-smelling. The bag seam contains no hidden pocket.

clues.title: An ivory outline
clues.text: Inside the damp patch lies a tile-sized square of glucose residue with two ivory paint flakes, one curved like the tail of a capital Q.

clues.title: One letter too glossy
clues.text: A photograph taken during the count shows a glossy Q among the matte wooden tiles. Celia's hand is beside it while Owen reaches for the sealing cord.

clues.title: The missing place card
clues.text: Celia brought hollow pulled-sugar place cards moulded to the exact tile dimensions. An unused card and a wooden tile both register three grams on the officials' scale. Her tray has an empty Q cavity, and matching ivory food paint dries on her pastry brush.

hints: The count can be correct even if one counted object is only pretending to be a wooden tile.
The tea did not remove anything through the sealed bag. It changed one water-soluble object already inside.

solution.title: The Q was counted, weighed, and then dissolved.
solution.explanation: Celia pocketed the wooden Q during counting and substituted a hollow painted sugar replica made in her tile-sized place-card mould. Its thin shell matched the wooden tile's three-gram reading, so it supplied the correct shape, count, and measured weight when Owen sealed the bag. Tea soaking through the canvas dissolved the false tile, leaving glucose and ivory food-paint flakes behind. The referee's photograph and Celia's empty Q mould identify the substitution.
proof: The intact seal means the bag contained the trick from the start
Sugar and Q-shaped paint remain in the damp patch
Celia made a matching sugar piece and handled it during counting

title: The Blank Kitchen Clue
subtitle: Dinner grew warmer. The handwriting quietly disappeared.
brief: At an apartment puzzle supper, the final handwritten clue was sealed in a clear box above the kitchen warming shelf. Everyone read it at 7:15. When the teams returned at 7:50, the card was blank although the box's paper lock remained intact.
Three organisers prepared the clue station. No one needed to reopen the box to make its message vanish.
question: Who made the clue disappear, and what ordinary change in the kitchen activated the trick?

suspects.name: Anika Shah
suspects.statement: I sealed the box, then switched on the warming shelf when dinner arrived.

suspects.name: Dev Linn
suspects.statement: I copied the clue using the permanent black pen Anika left beside the card.

suspects.name: Mira Bose
suspects.statement: I wrote the wording, but Dev made the display copy while I checked the answers.

theories.label: Lettered the card in heat-erasable ink that turned clear above the warming shelf
Rigged a white sheet inside the frame to slide over the writing as the box warmed
Placed a hidden cleaning capsule in the box whose vapour bleached ordinary ink

clues.title: Still sealed, still simple
clues.text: The paper lock and clear box are intact. Inside are only one card and two clips—no sliding sheet, capsule, thread, or mechanical part.

clues.title: Words without colour
clues.text: Side lighting reveals pen-pressure grooves spelling the original clue. The card was genuinely written on; the coloured ink alone became invisible.

clues.title: A warm little shelf
clues.text: After Anika switched it on, air around the clue box reached 54°C. Ordinary permanent ink remains black at that temperature.

clues.title: The letters return
clues.text: Held against a freezer pack, the card's dark violet words slowly reappear. Reversible heat-erasing ink can regain colour when chilled.

clues.title: The switched cap
clues.text: Dev's lettering case contains a violet heat-erasable tailoring pen fitted with the black cap from Anika's permanent marker. The permanent pen is in his case under Dev's violet cap.

hints: The grooves prove the words were not covered or removed. Only their colour changed.
Compare what happened near the warming shelf with what happens when the card is chilled again.

solution.title: The kitchen erased the clue on schedule.
solution.explanation: Dev switched pen caps and lettered the card with his violet heat-erasable tailoring pen while claiming to use Anika's permanent marker. Once the warming shelf raised the box to 54°C, the ink turned clear without anyone breaking the seal. The pressure grooves show the message was written, the freezer pack restores it, and the exchanged caps tie the deliberate substitution to Dev.
proof: The intact, empty mechanism rules out a physical cover
Heat erased the colour and cold restored it
Dev's switched pen caps reveal the deliberate ink swap
